records.title: Steering gear box repaired

fields.event: The storms having abated for a few hours, effected repairs. These repairs were made by Lieutenant R.S. Garvey, U.S.N.R. and Floyd C. Standlee, MoMM 2c, U.S.N. In their location, while so engaged, it would have taken several minutes to have gotten them inside the ship. Their intrepidity as well as skill are hereby cited. Their investigation revealed that, when steering from the bridge was removed during the last refit, two ball bearings, dropped into the bottom of the gear box and were not removed. These worked into the gears and caused jamming. Repairs were apparently a success.

records.title: Conning tower steering out

fields.event: The steering from the conning tower has been out for several days, difficulty suspected to be in the gear box forward of the conning tower, outside the pressure hull. We have been forced to wait for a lull in the succession of storms to investigate; meanwhile steering from the control room, not very efficient control.

records.title: Near collision with destroyer

fields.event: After one of several ten minute full speed runs in order to keep the true bearing from changing, put up the usual 8 feet of periscope and, fortunately, took first a quick look around in low power, for there was a destroyer with about zero angle on the bow, range about 2000 yards, all bow wave; probably about 25 knots. Sound had especially listened all around during the slow down and nothing had been heard. Naturally no tubes were ready. Made them ready at once but could not get a reasonable set up for a shot. Did not go deep though should have because all he had had to do was start dropping and we would have been badly off. The destroyer passed us us at about 200 yards range. She looked like the new Japanese type shown in the January 13, 1943 issue of "O.N.I. WEEKLY", similar to the USS ANDERSON.

fields.event: [SUMMARY] Fishing boats signaled target and escort. 19-knot chase ensued with escort closing slowly due to #4 main engine limits. Escort countered circle maneuver.

Escort turned on an extremely bright searchlight and commenced gunfire at 5300 yards. During the gunfire the escort apparently turned, for suddenly the radar lost contact. Attempted to regain contact and thereby be lead back to the target. Unsuccessful. Attempted then to search, regain contact and thereby attain favorable position for attack during the remainder of the night or at dawn. Attempts were unsuccessful.

records.title: Attack II A · Q-Ship

fields.narrative: Fired 3 bow torpedoes at 1900 yard range 110 port track. The first torpedo, which, if the problem was worked out correctly, should have hit, prematured in 15 seconds. The other two should have missed due to spread and did miss. The target turned toward us. Put up the periscope to give him a good point of aim and headed for him. Had only one torpedo ready forward because we try, normally, with only one old target, to save two dry torpedoes forward for the "coup de grace".

Narrative entry at 1726 K May 29 (page 6) describes this attack; its account is included here.

records.title: Attack II B · Q-Ship

fields.narrative: Fired one torpedo dead ahead zero angle on the bow torpedo run 800 yards, depth 15 feet (to avoid another premature though the sea was not rough). No detonation. Went deep at full speed and as much rudder as depth gaining could permit. As soon as we had gotten 60 degrees off the course shifted the rudder to pull the stern off the track. The first string of depth charges were beauties. A severe depth charging was the price we paid for this attack. If we could do it over again would have had more torpedoes ready and on the down the throat shot would have given him two at 15 feet and the last at zero foot depth to deliberately premature in his face. Might have blown his bow off. He had sound gear but did not ping. He was no amateur but made several runs and listened, just like a destroyer. He dropped about 20 charges in all.

fields.event: Last depth charge; not very close. Must be heavy ones because the usual swishing was more of a reverberation lasting nearly a minute. Our difficulty now is to get away. The current is equal to our one-third speed and setting us onto the islands of the IZU SHOTO. More speed means less battery.
Came to periscope depth a few minutes after sunset. Nothing in sight.
[SUMMARY] Cannot see through periscope. Came to 40 feet for SJ radar sweep: three echoes at 5000 yards. Went deep, altered course to put echoes abaft beam and worked sideways against current.

records.title: Attack III · Freighter

fields.narrative: Fired 3 bow torpedoes at the leading target, one hit about one-third of a ship's length inside of the stern. She was immediately down to the main deck aft and her screws stopped, never to start again. Started at once after the second target. We were close inshore, so close that the first firing had been to seaward. The second ship apparently decided we were to seaward and therefore tried to avoid us inshore. She was, however, changing course back and forth radically. Set up her average angle on the bow.

records.title: Attack IV B · Freighter

fields.narrative: Finally steady, our stern to his bow. Fired the last stern shot right down his throat. Went deep to avoid. No detonation. It is considered that the range was too close but had to take that chance. We fired as soon as we could and it could not have missed in deflection. Consider these four torpedoes wasted but they were worth the chance. We might have made a clean sweep. Listened to make sure that the target is by before we come up. Passed close aboard the sinking ship. We could hear him very clearly through our hull. Rather startling. Speeded up and turned away. We do not want him on top of us.

records.title: Attack V · Aircraft Carrier

fields.narrative: Fired 6 bow torpedoes at initial range of 1200 yards mean track 75 starboard using speed spread of 1 knot increments. At the time of firing we were inside the near screen, this vessel being at the moment on our port beam distance about 2000 yards, angle on the bow 30 port. By the time the hits started coming in which was just as the 6th fish was fired the angle on the bow of the nearest DD was almost zero. No time to turn to fire the stern anywhere. Went deep and stood by heading for the carrier. The target's screws had slowed and then stopped. Continued to head toward the target in order to confuse the depth chargers. We did not, however, have to wait long for their co-ordinated attacks, and they were excellent. As usual they alternated making runs and never wasted a charge.

fields.event: Crackling and popping sounds in the direction of the recent target. These were clearly audible through the hull almost as loud as those of June the first. At this time the co-ordinated depth charge attacks ceased and one destroyer depth charged for a while and then the other. Probably taking off survivors. However, the attacks were sufficiently persistent to keep us down. The crackling and depth charging continued until 2109.
Thought we were getting away so tried to get rid of some water. Screws and depth charges resulted. Then all quiet again.

Started up to periscope depth to try to get a look before the quarter moon set. However, had little hope of seeing much because our experience out here is that a quarter moon does not afford sufficient illumination.

records.title: Narrative entry

fields.event: Apparently could not see as well as we thought we could. Driven down again. No attack.
